cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and the room is getting calibrated as you go.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're doing for the people around you and one thing you're doing for you, out loud, where it can be heard.
cells.core:
You can hold what people feel without falling into it. Someone says something with an edge, and you take it in, you don't flinch, you don't grab an oar — you stay there until the temperature settles. That's a real skill and it's running now. When a table tips, people feel it even when they can't name it; you catch it in the shoulders, the pauses, the way a question lands differently than it was meant. You're reading the room and honoring it. You check yourself before you fire back. You know when to let silence sit.

The temptation is to hold so steadily that you stay standing while the others get a chair. Put your own need on the table loudly enough that it can be found — not to break the peace, but because a scale that drops its own side isn't fair to the person holding it. You can carry them and still say what you need. Say it.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the room in tune and vanish from the record.
cells.verb: holding space for what's felt without being swept off
cells.place: the table where things get set right between people

cells.tense: You are bracing for a disruption that has not arrived yet.
cells.ask: Let one person go one more round on their own before you step in.
cells.core: You're reading the room ahead of the room. Someone hasn't finished their sentence and you've already adjusted your posture, softened your voice, moved the salt away from a sore spot. That's care, but it's care on fast-forward — you're spending yourself on a version of the conversation that doesn't exist yet. Real closeness doesn't arrive pre-balanced. It gets arranged in real time, by both hands. When you manage the shape ahead of the fact, the other person doesn't get to find their own footing, and you don't get to find out whether they could. You already catch what's coming — you don't need to catch it twice. Let a moment go badly for two minutes and stay in it anyway. The braced posture is doing something real, but it's not holding the room. It's holding you at a distance.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding the room before it asks to be held.
cells.verb: holding space for what's felt without being swept off
cells.place: the table where things get set right between people

cells.tense: You are standing at a door that's already behind you.
cells.ask: Say out loud what you need from one person, before they ask you what you need.
cells.core: There's a way you used to be able to sit with someone's feeling and stay in the room. Somewhere that got parked. These days, when it matters, you go quiet or you go analytical, and the moment passes. You'd rather not test it — smart, but it also means you don't find out whether the thing is still there. It is; it just hasn't been fed. Connection isn't something you have or you don't. It's a muscle with a real, specific training: one conversation at a time, staying long enough for the other person to feel got, long enough for you to notice what you actually want to say. You don't need the whole room. You need one honest exchange where you don't manage it and you don't perform it. Pick a person you already trust to not need a performance. That's where the door opens.
cells.sheetLine: You have a door you've been walking past. You can open it.

cells.tense: You are holding the room, and calling it good manners.
cells.ask: Tell one person what you actually noticed, not just what would smooth the moment.
cells.core: You're doing the work — noticing the shift, changing your tone, giving the other person room to land. People can feel you doing it. They relax around you. What hasn't happened is you saying so. You'd call it being considerate, being polite, not making it weird. That's the blanket over it. Saying what you see isn't making it weird — it's the difference between being someone people are comfortable around and being someone people actually know. You read the moment already. Saying it out loud turns that reading into something the other person can answer. One sentence, in the moment, about what you noticed. It doesn't need to be a confession.
cells.sheetLine: The room is in your hands and you call it manners.
